meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Find what you love and let it kill you'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bukowski. Kinky Friedman coined “find what you like, and let it kill you” (1986); Van Dyke Parks swapped in “love” in 1998.

answer.label: Not Charles Bukowski — actually Kinky Friedman
answer.sourceLine: Bukowski is the internet’s favorite host for this line, but no poem, story, or letter of his contains it. Quote Investigator traces the adage to Texas humorist Kinky Friedman, quoted in a 1986 Houston Chronicle profile saying “find what you like, and let it kill you.” The now-famous “love” wording came later, from his friend Van Dyke Parks misremembering the line in a 1998 interview.

source.excerpt: “I’ve always said: Find what you like, and let it kill you.”
trail: The line is universally pinned to Charles Bukowski, but Quote Investigator found no poem, story, or letter of his that contains it.

The earliest evidence is a Sept. 18, 1986 Houston Chronicle profile in which humorist Kinky Friedman says “find what you like, and let it kill you.” His publicist later confirmed to the Houston Press that “Kinky has assured me it is a pure Kinky-ism.”
The “love” wording entered circulation when Friedman’s friend Van Dyke Parks paraphrased the line in a 1998 CMJ New Music Monthly interview, per Quote Investigator.
The Bukowski attribution appeared only in 2012 — eighteen years after his death — and hardened into a fabricated “letter” signed, tellingly, “~ Falsely yours,” as documented by QI.
source.excerptNote: Kinky Friedman’s original phrasing as documented in the 1986 Houston Chronicle profile. The widely shared “find what you love” version is Van Dyke Parks’ 1998 rewording, not Bukowski’s.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is a short spoken aphorism, not a line from any identifiable copyrighted Bukowski work — the Bukowski attribution is false. Its documented origins are a 1986 newspaper profile of Kinky Friedman and a 1998 magazine interview; short aphorisms like this generally fall outside copyright protection, so no clear rights status is asserted.

author.name: Kinky Friedman
author.heading: Who actually coined it
author.bio: Richard Samet “Kinky” Friedman was a Texas satirist who fronted the band Kinky Friedman and the Texas Jewboys before turning to comic detective novels and a Texas Monthly column. He ran an eccentric independent campaign for Texas governor in 2006. The aphorism “find what you like, and let it kill you” was, by his own account, a pure Kinky-ism — later softened into “love” and mistakenly handed to Bukowski.

misattribution.heading: How Bukowski got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet” misattribution: a punchy line drifts onto a famous edgy writer and sticks.

items.why: No poem, story, or letter by Bukowski contains this line. The credit first appeared online around April 21, 2012 — eighteen years after his 1994 death — and by December 2012 was wrapped in a fabricated “letter” signed “~ Falsely yours,” per Quote Investigator.

The catchy “find what you love” phrasing wasn’t Friedman’s original — his friend Van Dyke Parks introduced “love” while paraphrasing him in a 1998 CMJ New Music Monthly interview. Friedman’s own words used “like.”

misattribution.truthLine: The adage is Kinky Friedman’s — “find what you like, and let it kill you” (1986) — not Bukowski’s, as Quote Investigator and the Houston Press both established.

context.heading: Why the mix-up makes sense
lead: Bukowski — the poet of drink, ruin, and doomed devotion — is exactly the persona this line seems to belong to, which is precisely why it stuck to him. The sentiment fits his myth so snugly that few readers ever pause to ask for a page number.

But the trail runs to a different kind of Texan wit. Kinky Friedman delivered it as a wisecrack about betting his life on the things he loved; the more romantic “love” version is a friend’s fond misquotation that outgrew the original.
context.pull: “Kinky has assured me it is a pure Kinky-ism.”
